name: Belgian Tripel
title: Belgian Tripel: Style Guide | Craft Beer School
desc: Belgian Tripel: a strong, golden, dry Belgian ale. What it tastes like, why it hides its strength, food pairings and Indian examples.
tagline: Golden, strong and surprisingly dry. It drinks lighter than its 8 to 9 percent.
tastes:
Tripel is the strong golden ale of the Belgian abbey tradition, brought to its modern form at Westmalle in the 1930s. It looks like a pale lager and carries the strength of a fortified wine, which is exactly why it catches people out. The trick is sugar. Brewers add plain white or candi sugar to a pale malt base, and the yeast turns it into alcohol without leaving body behind. The result is a beer that sits around 8 to 9 percent but finishes dry and almost crisp.

The flavour is mostly yeast and malt in balance. Expect banana, pear and orange from the esters, a peppery, clove-like spice, soft honeyed malt and a firm but quiet bitterness from noble hops. Alcohol shows as a gentle warmth, never as solvent or heat. A hot, boozy tripel usually means fermentation ran away without temperature control. A good one is lively, bottle conditioned and dangerous in the most polite way.

profile.look: Deep yellow to rich gold, bright to slightly hazy from bottle conditioning, with a dense, long-lasting white head.
profile.aroma_flavour: Spicy phenols and pear, banana and orange esters over soft, honeyed pale malt. A light herbal hop note and gentle alcohol warmth.
profile.mouthfeel: Medium-light body for its strength, high carbonation, and a dry, slightly bitter finish with a little warmth.
profile.ingredients: Pilsner malt, a good share of white or candi sugar, noble hops such as Saaz or Styrian Golding, and a Belgian abbey yeast.

in_india: Tripel is a beer to treat with respect in Indian heat. It is strong, and a cold, fizzy glass on a hot afternoon goes down faster than its alcohol deserves, so pour it in small measures. It travels reasonably well because of its strength, but bottles left in a hot godown lose their freshness and turn honeyed and dull. Goa has a packaged example, and Bengaluru brewpubs pour one now and then. It suits a slow dinner or a wedding toast better than a session.

pairings.why: The beer's carbonation and dry finish clear the ghee, and its spice meets the whole garam masala.
Rich, creamy gravy is cut by the bubbles, while the honeyed malt sits comfortably with the cashew.
Nutty, crystalline cheese and a strong golden ale share a sweetness without either taking over.
The beer's dryness stops the sweet from cloying, and the cashew picks up the soft malt.
